title: Research
text:
My research focuses on genetic modeling, which consists in building a representation of how inheritance determines the expression of phenotypes. Inheritance was long studied through the mere relatedness between individuals. Genomic markers, then whole genome sequencing, now provide an increasingly complete picture of its physical support. This information, together with the growth of computational means, opens new challenges for genetic modeling.
The goals of my research are, on the one hand, to optimize the efficiency of breeding, and, on the other hand, to understand how the genome expresses from a more fundamental perspective.
All my work can be read as successive answers to one question:


How to estimate, and how to interpret, the genetic variances and covariances between traits when their number grows?


Each phenotypic trait has a genetic variance, which tells how much it can respond to selection. Each pair of traits shares a genetic covariance, which tells how selecting on one trait moves the other. Gathered over a set of traits, these quantities form a genetic covariance matrix. In breeding, this matrix tells how much leverage selection has on each trait and how traits constrain each other. The notion of trait can be stretched: the same phenotype measured in different environments, or the parameters describing its response along a gradient (such as temporal or environmental), can all be handled as distinct traits.
As my research progressed, this matrix kept growing, and with it a statistical difficulty: the number of parameters grows quadratically with the number of traits, and their estimation quickly becomes unstable, then impossible.
The following sections retrace these steps, and what each of them required:

Section 1 recalls the core concepts of quantitative genetics and the genetic mixed model, the tool used to estimate these variances and covariances.
Section 2 extends the matrix across traits: bivariate genomic prediction, then a 6-trait Bayesian model and the behavior of its priors.
Section 3 extends it along an environmental gradient: random regression, and what it reveals about plasticity, heterosis and trade-offs between traits.
Section 4 reduces it, either a posteriori by collapsing several traits into a single index, either a priori by limiting the estimation to the principal components of the covariance (factor analytic).
Section 5 presents pyreml, a differentiable mixed model solver running on GPU, and the open question of how far mixed models and neural networks can be joined.

title: Research
text:
1 Modeling phenotypes

1.1 Core quantitative genetics concepts
If we were to identify a single starting point to the science of quantitative genetics, it would be Fisher’s seminal paper (Fisher 1918), which simultaneously: reconciled Mendelian genetics with the Darwinian theory of evolution; identified the relevance of reasoning with variances and coined the concept of heritability; and proposed the analysis of variance, which is both the first genetic model and a foundation of modern statistics. In a nutshell, the central limit theorem allows countless infinitesimal effects with a Mendelian inheritance to explain the continuous distribution of quantitative traits, which fits the Darwinian view of how natural selection shapes species.
From its very origin, quantitative genetics is therefore both a statistical and an evolutionary discipline. This dual nature runs through all that follows.
Reasoning with variances:
\[
\sigma^2_P = \sigma^2_G + \sigma^2_E,
\qquad
H^2 = \frac{\sigma^2_G}{\sigma^2_P},
\]
with \(\sigma^2_P\) the phenotypic variance, \(\sigma^2_G\) the genetic variance and \(\sigma^2_E\) the environmental variance. \(H^2\) is the broad-sense heritability. From this fundamental equation have been derived:

\(\sigma^2_P = \sigma^2_G + \sigma^2_E + \sigma^2_{G \times E}\) (Falconer 1989), with a genotype-by-environment interaction variance component.
\(\sigma^2_G = \sigma^2_A + \sigma^2_D + \sigma^2_I\) (Falconer 1989), with respectively the additive, dominance and epistatic variances; and \(h^2 = \sigma^2_A / \sigma^2_P\) the narrow-sense heritability.
\(\sigma^2_G = \sigma^2_{A_\alpha} + \sigma^2_{A_\beta} + \sigma^2_{D}\) (Comstock et al. 1949; Stuber and Cockerham 1966), specific to the hybrid breeding context, with the additive variances associated with the general combining abilities (GCA) of two heterotic groups \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), and the dominance variance associated with the specific combining ability (SCA) of each hybrid family.

Accessing the narrow-sense heritability (or a partial heritability per heterotic group in the latter case) is pivotal in breeding, as it determines the efficiency of selection as given by the breeder’s equation \(R = \rho\,\sigma_A\,i\), with \(R\) the response to selection, \(\rho\) the accuracy (\(\rho = h\) when selecting directly on phenotypes), and \(i\) the selection intensity. The same equation describes the response of a natural population to selection; only the origin of the selective pressure differs.



1.2 The genetic mixed model
Fisher had the intuition of working on variances, but did not exploit it to its full extent. Henderson (Henderson 1949; Henderson 1975) introduced the linear mixed model (LMM), which effectively implemented and fully leveraged random effects in Fisher’s ANOVA model. For an accessible introduction to LMM random effects, see for instance pyreml’s doc (Marchal, Trottier, et al. 2026).
Considering a basic genetic LMM:
\[
y_i = \mu + a_i + r_i,
\qquad
a \sim N(0, \sigma^2_A \mathbf{A}),
\qquad
r \sim N(0, \sigma^2_R \mathbf{I}),
\]
with \(y\) a phenotypic trait, \(\mu\) the population mean, \(a_i\) the breeding value of individual \(i\), \(r_i\) a residual of variance \(\sigma^2_R\) and \(\mathbf{I}\) an identity matrix. The breeding value is conceptually close to the additive effect sensu stricto, but it also encompasses the average effect of non-additive components over the population, given the distribution of allele frequencies, i.e. the genetic background of the population. The variances (\(\sigma^2_A\), \(\sigma^2_R\)) are estimated in a computationally intensive step, the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) (Patterson and Thompson 1971; Harville 1977).
Considering \(a\) as random has 2 major advantages:

\(a\) is a best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP), which means it is shrunk (or regularized, in machine learning terminology). This allows fitting a largely under-determined system and maximizes the generalizability of the inference.
The covariance of \(a\) has a known structure \(\mathbf{A}\), the kinship, built either from the pedigree (Malécot 1948; Mrode and Thompson 2005) or from molecular information (Meuwissen et al. 2001; VanRaden 2008).

In the latter case, the model is called a genomic BLUP (GBLUP) and is often based on markers such as SNPs. Noteworthily, the markers do not have to be causal: the effect of causal QTLs is captured by the linkage disequilibrium between them and the markers.
Two features of this model matter for the rest of this page. First, the kinship is nothing more than a similarity matrix between individuals: in machine learning terms, a kernel. Nothing in the model requires that this similarity come from genetics, which is what we exploit in Section 4.3. Second, the variances are not a by-product of the fit: they are the quantities of interest, because they carry the biological meaning (heritability, genetic correlations). This is why I care so much about estimating them without bias, all the way to Section 5.
The genetic LMM, based on either pedigree or markers, and the concepts behind it, frame my research.

title: Research
text:
2 Phenotypes are multivariate
My first research topic took place in the context of hybrid oil palm breeding, where I focused on the performance of bivariate modeling (Cros 2014; Marchal 2014; Marchal et al. 2016).
I then continued in perennial crop breeding with a PhD on a hybrid forest tree: the European \(\times\) Japanese larch. Phenotypes are multivariate, and the full picture is essential for the breeder to make informed decisions: the heritability of each trait tells how much leverage is available, and the genetic correlations act as a constraint system, as selecting on one trait impacts all the others. The goal of the first chapter of my PhD was to draw this full picture for hybrid larch, estimating all genetic parameters along with heterosis and in relation to G\(\times\)E interactions (Marchal et al. 2017, 2019; Marchal 2018).
In this section, I present the multivariate genetic model used in both research projects, then how bivariate modeling improves hybrid oil palm breeding, and finally how high-dimensional modeling was achieved during my PhD.

2.1 Multivariate genetic mixed model
All my experience in breeding concerned primarily hybrid crops. Here, the parents of the hybrids were heterozygous populations (for oil palm) or species (for larch). The model presented here is designed for these specificities (Stuber and Cockerham 1966; Cros 2014; Marchal 2018):
\[
\begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_p \end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \mu_2 \\ \vdots \\ \mu_p \end{pmatrix} +
\begin{pmatrix} g_{\alpha1} \\ g_{\alpha2} \\ \vdots \\ g_{\alpha p} \end{pmatrix} +
\begin{pmatrix} g_{\beta1} \\ g_{\beta2} \\ \vdots \\ g_{\beta p} \end{pmatrix} +
\begin{pmatrix} s_{1} \\ s_{2} \\ \vdots \\ s_{p} \end{pmatrix} +
\begin{pmatrix} r_1 \\ r_2 \\ \vdots \\ r_p \end{pmatrix},
\]
with:

\(y_j\) the phenotype \(j\) of average \(\mu_j\);
\(g_{\alpha j}\), \(g_{\beta j}\) and \(s_{j}\) the GCA of group \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), and the SCA respectively;
\(r_j\) the residual.

Both the genetic effects and the residual are taken as random:
\[
g_\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{\Sigma}_\alpha \otimes \mathbf{K}_\alpha)
\qquad
g_\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{\Sigma}_\beta \otimes \mathbf{K}_\beta)
\qquad
s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{\Sigma}_D \otimes \mathbf{D})
\qquad
r \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{\Sigma}_R \otimes \mathbf{I})
\]
with \(\mathbf{K}_\alpha\) and \(\mathbf{K}_\beta\) built from pedigree, molecular markers or both (Legarra et al. 2009); and \(\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{K}_\alpha \otimes \mathbf{K}_\beta\) (Lynch and Walsh 1998; Ovaskainen et al. 2008). All the covariance matrices \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_\alpha\), \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_\beta\), \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_D\) and \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_R\) are full and contain \((p^2 + p) /2\) elements to estimate. Because the biological models (oil palm populations, larch species) are heterozygous (unlike, for instance, maize or Arabidopsis thaliana fixed lines), Mendelian segregation is involved (full sibs are not clones):

\(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\alpha\,jj} =½\,\sigma^2_{A\alpha\,j}\),
\(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\beta\,jj} = ½\,\sigma^2_{A\beta\,j}\),
\(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{D\,jj} = ¼\,\sigma^2_{D\,j}\),

with the residual capturing the individual genetic variation, i.e. the remaining \(½\) of the additive variance and \(¾\) of the dominance variance. Finally, any genetic correlation (additive \(r_{A\alpha}\) and \(r_{A\beta}\), or dominance \(r_{D}\)) is straightforwardly obtained as:
\[
r_{ij} = \frac{\mathbf{\Sigma}_{ij}}{\sqrt{\mathbf{\Sigma}_{ii}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{jj}}}.
\]


2.2 Bivariate modeling improves the analysis accuracy
GBLUP may benefit from multivariate modeling, especially for strongly correlated traits with unbalanced heritabilities or missing values (Calus and Veerkamp 2011; Jia and Jannink 2012; Guo et al. 2014). During my internship at Cirad, I analyzed a hybrid oil palm progeny test laid out as an incomplete factorial, located in North Sumatra, whose data had been collected over 5 years. At the time of the study, the oil palms had been genotyped with SSRs, and a significant part of the research consisted in adapting GBLUP to multi-allelic markers. I focused on two elementary components of oil yield, known to be strongly correlated: the number of bunches (BN) and their average weight (ABW).
We can distinguish two accuracies. On the one hand, the selection accuracy \(cor(u, \hat{u})\) for a given genetic value \(u\) (GCA from group \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\), or SCA) was derived from the model prediction error variances. The selection accuracy matters most to the breeder, as it is \(\rho\) in the breeder’s equation \(R = \rho\,\sigma_A\,i\) when selecting from a GBLUP model. On the other hand, I also considered the prediction accuracy \(cor(y, \hat{G})\), with \(\hat{G}\) the predicted total genetic value (i.e. the sum of all genetic components).
The main result is summarized in Figure 1: bivariate modeling of BN and ABW brought a large and significant improvement of the selection accuracy for GCA. This result was also confirmed for the SCA of observed and non-observed hybrid combinations. The two traits are strongly (negatively) correlated, which partly explains this result. However, unlike the textbook cases of the literature, BN and ABW show no extreme pattern of missing values or of heritabilities (heritabilities range from 0.23 to 0.57, Cros et al. 2015). Multivariate modeling can thus improve GBLUP selection accuracy even in this configuration.






Figure 1: Improvement in the GCA selection accuracy for both heterotic groups A and B, and for both traits BN and ABW, when using a bivariate GBLUP instead of a univariate one (from Marchal et al. 2016).



I also carried out a cross-validation, which did not confirm a gain in prediction accuracy (Marchal 2014). This is less contradictory than it seems: the model’s main goal is not to brute-force predict the phenotype \(y\), but to obtain the most accurate representation of its genetic components. The most conclusive test would be to observe how selection decisions based on univariate and bivariate models perform in a new generation, thus actually applying the breeder’s equation to assess \(\rho\) a posteriori.


2.3 High dimension modeling: the “full picture”
In the previous section, I expanded from a univariate to a bivariate model to gain accuracy. In the context of my PhD at INRAE-Orléans, my goal was different: estimating the whole genetic correlation structure for its own sake, as it is key information for breeding. The hybrid larch progeny test was a full diallel between 9 European larches (Larix decidua) and 9 Japanese larches (L. kaempferi), observed on 3 sites in an incomplete block design. Being a diallel, it included all 3 taxa (both parental species and the hybrid). I first fitted a univariate model to account for spatial effects within each site, including all taxa for a complete spatial representation. Then, I performed the multivariate analyses of 6 phenotypic traits taxon by taxon, with a GCA model for the hybrids. I used the latest measurements available: the trees had been growing since 1997 on sites SA and SS and since 2004 on site PC, with regular phenotyping campaigns. No markers were available, so all kinships were pedigree-based.
In oil palm breeding, fitting the bivariate model with ASReml (Gilmour et al. 2009; Butler et al. 2009) had been very challenging, likely because of genetic correlations close to \(-1\). The Average Information (AI) algorithm implemented in ASReml is also sensitive to starting values and prone to derail. A 6-trait model was out of reach for this approach. To fit it, I tuned a Bayesian framework based on the R package MCMCglmm (Hadfield 2010), implementing Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). MCMCglmm relies on prior–posterior conjugacy, which constrains the prior of the covariance matrix to an inverse-Wishart. For this reason, I investigated the prior hyperparameterization in depth (Gelman 2006; Gelman and Hill 2007; Sorensen and Gianola 2007). I also used parameter expansion (PX, Liu et al. 1998; Hadfield 2016) to speed up computation and obtain less autocorrelated Markov chains. However, to my knowledge, the effect of PX on the marginal priors of variances and correlations had never been assessed. Using simulation, I confirmed that:

the marginal prior for variances was nearly flat and monotonic (not biasing towards a particular value) (Figure 2a);
the marginal prior for correlations was perfectly flat on \(]-1,1[\) (Figure 2b).







Figure 2: Marginal prior for the variances (a) and the correlations (b), from a PX inverse-Wishart (\(p = 6\) dimensions, \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I_6}\), \(\nu = p + 1 = 7\)), and PX hyperparameters \(\mathbf{V_\alpha} = 1000\,\mathbf{I_6}\), \(\mu_\alpha = 0\) (from Marchal 2018)



After obtaining apparently converged Markov chains, I could draw the full inference over all genetic parameters, including all genetic correlations between traits, as summarized in Figure 3. Based on the 95% credible intervals (CI), some of these correlations were significantly different from \(0\), notably between BHC and HT, and between HT and DEN, indicating that taller trees tend to be both larger and denser. This is good news for breeding: these 3 traits, all with a positive economic value, can be improved together.






Figure 3: Genetic additive correlations between 6 traits of interest for larch breeding: breast-height circumference (BHC), height (HT), wood density (DEN), heartwood proportion (HWP), stem flexuosity (FLX), bud flush phenology (BUD); observed in 3 sites (SA, SS, PC); either in pure species (E and J for European and Japanese larch respectively) or in hybridization (HE and HJ respectively) (from Marchal et al. 2017).



One difficulty met here stayed with me: with 6 traits, each covariance matrix already holds 21 parameters, and their number grows quadratically with the number of traits. Some of these models took weeks to run, and as traits are added, estimating all parameters both fast and reliably becomes out of reach, which calls for more parsimonious structures such as the factor-analytic model (Section 4.2).

title: Research
text:
3 Phenotypes are plastic
Phenotypic plasticity is a broad topic, covering all possible cases of G\(\times\)E interaction. As a textbook illustration, queen and worker bees show no specific genetic difference, and their caste is determined by the food they receive as larvae. We focus here on how the environment shapes the phenotypes of plants. Though not as categorical as caste determination in hymenopterans, plasticity is of singular importance in plants, which by definition cannot escape the soil and weather they are exposed to throughout their life thus are constrained to adapt to it.

3.1 Modeling plasticity
G\(\times\)E interactions can be tackled from two modeling perspectives, which correspond to the two classical views of plasticity in evolutionary biology (Schlichting and Pigliucci 1998).
The first perspective considers the phenotypes observed in different environments as different traits, as announced in the introduction. It therefore relies on a discrete definition of the environment, and it can be handled with a multivariate genetic model, except for the residual, for which \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_R\) reduces to a diagonal matrix (different environments share no observation, hence no residual correlation). This is common in agriculture, where the same genotypes are observed in a multi-environment trial network (MET). In this view, a genetic correlation lower than \(1\) between two environments is precisely G\(\times\)E.
The second perspective considers the environment as continuous instead of discrete. The phenotype is then better described by a function along the environmental covariate, i.e. a reaction norm. This view was central to my PhD, and led me to a 3-month research visit to Carl Schlichting’s laboratory (University of Connecticut, Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology). Modeling these reaction norms raises a colinearity problem as soon as we try to model curvature. The most straightforward idea would be to model the phenotype as a polynomial of the environmental factor, e.g. of order 3: \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 e^1 + \beta_2 e^2 + \beta_3 e^3\). By construction, \(e\) and \(e^2\) often show extremely high correlation. Centering \(e\) around \(0\) makes \(cor(e, e^2) = 0\), but it does not fix \(cor(e, e^3)\), which remains high. The problem worsens with higher order polynomials and calls for a systematic solution. One solution consists in using Legendre polynomials, which are mutually orthogonal at any order on \([-1, 1]\) (Kirkpatrick et al. 1990; Schaeffer 2004; Meyer and Kirkpatrick 2005). Let us consider \(\mathcal{L}_m(e)\), the \(m^\text{th}\) Legendre polynomial applied to \(e\) after a linear transformation bringing all \(e\)’s to \([-1, 1]\).

The random regression genetic model can then be defined (neglecting the SCA for parsimony):
\[
y_{ijklt} =
  \sum^{M_b}_{m=0} b_{m} \mathcal{L}_m(e_t) +
  \sum^{M_\alpha}_{m=0} g_{\alpha\,im} \mathcal{L}_m(e_t) +
  \sum^{M_\beta}_{m=0} g_{\beta\,jm} \mathcal{L}_m(e_t) +
  \sum^{M_p}_{m=0} p_{km} \mathcal{L}_m(e_t) +
  r_{ijklt}
\]
with \(y_{ijklt}\) the \(l^\text{th}\) observation of individual \(k\), of parents \(i\) and \(j\), at the \(t^\text{th}\) point of the environmental gradient. The population reaction norm is given by \(b\), the only fixed part of the model. There is now one GCA \(g\) per heterotic group \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) and per polynomial order \(m\). Each order \(M_b, M_\alpha, M_\beta\) and \(M_p\) could theoretically be tuned independently. The permanent environment effect \(p_{km}\) captures all individual variation not captured by the modeled genetic components. The random effects follow:

\(g_\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{\Sigma}_\alpha)\), and likewise for \(g_\beta\);
\(p \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{\Sigma}_p)\).

The residual \(r\) is i.i.d. Here, \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_\alpha\) is a covariance between the intercept, slope and curvature of the reaction norms: the same object as in the multivariate model, where “traits” are now polynomial coefficients. As for the multivariate genetic model, the challenging part remains the estimation of dense \(\mathbf{\Sigma}\)’s with \((p^2 + p) /2\) variance components. Consequently, the Bayesian framework that we designed for high-dimensional multivariate models can be used for random regression as well. The two approaches (random regression and multivariate modeling) can also be combined, as we did in the following sections; see for instance pyreml’s doc (Marchal, Trottier, et al. 2026).
Though conceptually elegant, this model has statistical limitations:

It requires many parameters, and in practice the first orders (those that do not require Legendre polynomials) are often sufficient.
Modeling the residual \(r\) as independent of \(e\) is almost always a questionable choice. Modeling heteroscedasticity, as pyreml allows (Marchal, Trottier, et al. 2026), is pivotal to remain within the linear model assumptions in random regression.
The model extrapolates very poorly, even within \([-1, 1]\), which can produce misleading insights, especially when \(e\) does not start and end at the same point for all individuals.



3.2 Role of phenotypic plasticity in the construction of hybrid larch heterosis
As they grow exceptionally old and record variation in their growth rings, trees are a window to the past. This is especially interesting as their growth correlates with past climatic events. This section focuses on sites SA and SS of the experimental set-up previously described. Wood cores were sampled from each tree, reduced to a standard thickness and X-rayed to obtain a microdensitometric profile (Figure 4). Two traits were analyzed, for a given sample and a given year: ring width (RW) and ring mean density (RMD).






Figure 4: Microdensitometric profile (on top), obtained from the radiography (in the middle) of a wood core sample (at the bottom) (from Marchal et al. 2019).



To describe the environment, I developed a daily water availability model inspired by the closed-source, licensed model BILJOU© (Granier et al. 1999; Bréda et al. 2006; Marchal et al. 2019), adapted to the specificities of our trial: the leaf area index (LAI) varies over time, and the available water capacity (AWC) varies spatially. Neither was covered by BILJOU©. I estimated the increasing LAI over time from tree circumferences, measured throughout their growth. We measured AWC at contrasting locations of each site from soil pits, and I interpolated it using tree height BLUPs as a proxy. Finally, I summarized the information at the year level with “D1rew”, defined as the first decile of the daily relative extractable water (REW) in a given year. D1rew explained more phenotypic variance (about twice as much for RW) than “MJJA”, a simpler index built as the sum of precipitation during the growing season (May to August). Building the environmental axis is an important part of the model: a poorly defined gradient yields poorly defined reaction norms.
The core question of my PhD was the role of phenotypic plasticity in the construction of hybrid larch heterosis. To address it, I fitted an order 3 random regression model across sites SA and SS for each taxon (L. decidua, L. kaempferi or their hybrid). The fixed part of the model, i.e. the average reaction norm of each taxon within each site, is presented in Figure 5. On the one hand, heterosis (hybrid superiority) was expressed in RW, and was stronger with higher D1rew, i.e. higher water availability, a more favorable environment. Interestingly, the ranking between European and Japanese larches varied between sites for RW, but the hybrid always ranked first. On the other hand, the reaction norms of RMD were flat with respect to D1rew, the ranking between taxa was constant, and the hybrid displayed the average value of its parents, i.e. no heterosis.






Figure 5: Reaction norms of RW (a, c) and RMD (b, d) along the environmental covariate D1rew, in the sites SA (a-b) and SS (c-d), for each taxon: European larch (in blue), Japanese larch (in red) and their hybrid (in green). Dashed lines: 95% credible intervals (from Marchal et al. 2019)



Heterosis is thus not a static property of the hybrid: it is itself a plastic trait.


3.3 Genetic parameters as longitudinal functions
To estimate all genetic variance parameters, I fitted an order 1 bivariate (RW + RMD) random regression model across sites, for each taxon. From the random regression perspective, the breeding values and GCAs, as well as all genetic variances and parameters derived from them, can be interpreted as functions of the environmental gradient (D1rew) (Figure 6, Figure 7, Figure 8). The Japanese larch showed more contrasted results, and for simplicity this section focuses on this taxon only.






Figure 6: Narrow-sense heritabilities along D1rew for Japanese larch, for the traits: RW (c) and RMD (d). Black line: heritability in pure species crosses; and grey line: heritability in hybridization. Dashed lines: 95% credible intervals (from Marchal et al. 2019).



The heritability of RW was extremely low, whereas the heritability of RMD was estimable (around \(h^2 = 0.10\)), with a slight though non-significant trend to increase with higher D1rew (Figure 6). The heritability was identical in hybridization and in pure species breeding. The additive genetic correlation between RW and RMD, however, showed a clear pattern: positive or null (CI encompassing 0) at lower D1rew, it switched abruptly to negative at higher D1rew (Figure 7). The correlations in pure species and in hybridization both displayed this trend, though the negative correlation became significant (excluding 0) only in pure species.






Figure 7: Additive genetic correlation between RW and RMD along D1rew, for Japanese larch. Black line: correlation in pure species crosses; and grey line: correlation in hybridization. Dashed lines: 95% credible intervals (from Marchal et al. 2019).



These genetic variance parameters summarize the distribution of the genetic performances (breeding values and GCAs) of the founders of the genetic trials (Figure 8). The genetic performances were more contrasted for RMD and tended to diverge with higher D1rew, in agreement with the trend observed for the heritability. In hybridization, RW also expressed some variability at high D1rew, and the best performers in RW were lower in RMD, illustrating the emergence of a negative additive genetic correlation between these traits. Notably, founders 3179 and 3180 expressed the most contrasted patterns. Though not represented here, some of these contrasts between founders were significant for both traits at high D1rew (Marchal et al. 2019).






Figure 8: Genetic performances with 95% CIs (dashed lines) for some contrasted Japanese larch parents for RW (e, f) and RMD (g, h), in pure species (breeding value) (e, g) and in hybridization (twice the GCA) (f, h), along D1rew. Each color represents one genotype, labeled in the legend on the right (from Marchal et al. 2019).



In a nutshell, the expression of all genetic contrasts was conditional on water availability: heterosis at the taxon level in growth (RW), and individual performances, especially in density (RMD). With high D1rew, a trade-off emerged between RW and RMD, which can be read as follows: favorable conditions are converted either into more wood (RW) or into denser wood (RMD), and genotypes differ in which way they go.
Here, favorable conditions revealed genetic differences, and with them a genetic constraint between two traits that was invisible under drought. For the breeder, this means that the genetic parameters estimated in one environment may not hold in another, and that the selection strategy itself should depend on the target environment.

title: Research
text:
4 Tackling the complexity


What is simple is false, what is complicated is unusable. — Paul Valéry


In the previous sections, the genetic covariance matrices (\(\mathbf{\Sigma}_\alpha\), \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_\beta\), \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_D\)) kept growing: across traits in multivariate modeling, across intercept, slope and higher order components in random regression, and sometimes both. From now on, let us write \(\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\) for any of them, so that the genetic value \(a\) follows \(a \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{\Sigma_a} \otimes \mathbf{A})\), with \(\mathbf{A}\) the kinship. In line with the introduction, a “trait” is any element with an entry in \(\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\): a distinct phenotypic trait, the regression coefficient of a trait on a covariate, or its expression in an environment taken as discrete.
This section tackles the reduction of \(\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\) in two ways. A posteriori, once \(\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\) is estimated, a selection index collapses all traits into a single one, so that a breeder can make simple decisions in a complex context. A priori, the factor-analytic model constrains the estimation itself to a few principal components, which makes large \(\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\) estimable at all.

4.1 Back to a single trait
We have already mentioned that, in the presence of genetic correlations, selecting on trait 1 also impacts trait 2. Let \(r_A\) be the additive genetic correlation between both traits; the correlated response of trait 2 when selecting on trait 1 is then \(R_2 = h_1\,r_A\,\sigma_{A2}\,i\) (Falconer 1989). In breeding, these correlations may be favorable (both traits vary in the desired direction) or, more often, adverse. In the latter case, a trade-off is required that accounts for the correlation constraints between traits and for their relative importance. Selection indices collapse the complex multivariate system into a single trait that can be directly used for selection. On the one hand, an index accounts simultaneously for all trade-offs between the traits. On the other hand, it reduces the complexity of phenotypic gains, so that the breeder can focus on other concerns, such as the preservation of genetic diversity. The Smith-Hazel index (Smith 1936; Hazel 1943; Lynch and Walsh 1998) is particularly concise: \(b = \mathbf{\Sigma_a}^{-1}\,d\), with \(b\) the index weights, \(d\) a vector of desired gains, designed for instance from the economic importance of each trait, and \(\Delta\) the mean of the fraction selected by truncation on the index in the widget below. Because the index weights depend directly on \(\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\), the index is the most direct illustration of how genetic covariances shape the joint response of several traits to selection. In evolutionary terms, the same matrix shapes and constrains the joint response of a population to natural selection.



4.2 The factor-analytic model
The selection index acts a posteriori: it projects a multivariate system onto a single axis, and assumes that both \(\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\) (used to design the index) and the breeding values or GCAs (upon which the projection applies) have been successfully estimated and predicted. The estimation step itself, however, can be very challenging in high dimension: the number of elementary variance parameters grows quadratically, \((p^2 + p) /2\), and is constrained by the positive-definiteness of \(\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\). As \(p\) grows, the variance parameters quickly become unidentifiable. The factor-analytic (FA) model tackles this problem (Smith et al. 2001; Kirkpatrick and Meyer 2004; Meyer 2009) by focusing on the estimation of the latent structure of a reduced-rank \(\mathbf{\Sigma_a} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^\top
+ \mathbf{\Psi},\) with \(\mathbf{Q}_{p \times q}\) an orthonormal matrix of \(q\) principal components, \(q \ll p\), \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) the eigenvalue-like importance of each axis, and \(\mathbf{\Psi}\) the diagonal specificity matrix.
Frequentist FA mixed models are implemented in ASReml (Gilmour et al. 2009) and Wombat (Meyer 2006), both closed-source. FA has also been investigated in a Bayesian framework, using conjugate distributions (Nuvunga et al. 2019). At Seenovate, I hired and supervised an MSc intern to explore the core algorithmic steps of an FA implementation in a Bayesian framework with stan, whose no-U-turn sampler (NUTS) freed us from conjugacy constraints (Marchal, Lamure, et al. 2026). At CNRS, I then implemented this algorithm in a frequentist, open-source REML solver (Marchal, Trottier, et al. 2026).
The Bayesian FA research had 2 goals. The first was methodological: exploring an FA algorithm, implementing it in both a Gaussian and a negative-binomial generalized mixed model, and studying its sensitivity to the priors (Figure 9). The second, replacing the kinship with neural network embeddings, is presented in Section 4.3.






Figure 9: Prior sensitivity of the Bayesian factor-analytic Gaussian mixed model, using a centered half-Gaussian distributions for the elements of \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) with varying dispersion \(\sigma^2_\lambda\), all other hyperparameters kept constant. The FA1 and FA2 accuracies (\(r_{FA}\)) are the correlations of the columns of \(\hat{\mathbf{Q}}\) with the ground-truth, simulated \(\mathbf{Q}\). The clustering match is defined as the match between the estimated and the ground-truth clusters of the simulation, from a 2-clusters segmentation. \(R^2_{FA}\) is the proportion of variance captured by \(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^\top\) in opposition to \(\mathbf{\Psi}\) (from Marchal, Lamure, et al. 2026).



Retrieving the latent structure can be a goal in itself: more than a computational trick reducing the number of parameters to estimate, the latent structure can be considered meaningful on its own. In quantitative genetics, its leading axes are the directions of the trait space along which most genetic variance lies, i.e. the directions along which selection, artificial or natural, is most effective. For this reason, Figure 9 focuses on the retrieval of a simulated latent structure. The model proved able to retrieve the latent structure under some hyperparameterizations, but showed a strong sensitivity to the prior.
I then implemented the FA model in a frequentist framework (pyreml, Marchal, Trottier, et al. 2026) and benchmarked it against the state-of-the-art, reference software Wombat (Meyer 2006, 2009). Switching from Bayesian to frequentist removed the question of prior sensitivity. The benchmark was carried out on the Arabidopsis thaliana 1001 genomes and the easyGWAS trait collection (Alonso-Blanco et al. 2016; Grimm et al. 2017), and the resulting estimated correlation circle is presented in Figure 10.






Figure 10: Correlation circle of A. thaliana traits, as directly inferred in a FA mixed model using pyreml, and which is consistent to the one estimated using Wombat (from Marchal, Trottier, et al. 2026)



As far as I know, this is the first open-source REML implementation of the FA mixed model. When adjusting pyreml convergence criterion to meet Wombat’s, both software led to the same estimates, which validated the algorithmic approach. pyreml, running on GPU (A100), was then 4 times faster than Wombat running on 64 CPUs.


4.3 Beyond genetic relatedness
The second goal of the Bayesian FA research was to demonstrate that the genomic kinship could be replaced by a kernel built from the embeddings of an encoder neural network (Marchal, Lamure, et al. 2026). Since the kinship is only a similarity matrix, the genetic framework extends to a broad variety of applications: encoders can provide a relatedness matrix between images, sounds, texts, sentiments, etc., and the mixed model can interpret these representations analytically through a variance decomposition. We illustrated this by analyzing how much of the number of citations of research papers is explained by their title, as encoded by a natural language processing model. The amount of variance explained was low, for several likely reasons:

The negative-binomial model extracts little information from the data, as shown in the simulations.
Our approach was naive and did not account for the many other factors influencing the number of citations.
The encoder was taken as is, and was not fine-tuned to make its embeddings more explanatory.

Still, despite being low, the variance explained by the title was significant in cross-validation, which proves the concept. Concerning the last point, the mixed model and the encoder should ideally be trained together, on the same task. This is the starting point of my current research at CNRS (Section 5).

title: Research
text:
5 Current interests
In Section 4.3, I applied mixed-effect modeling to a kernel obtained from text embeddings. Conceptually, the encoder and the mixed model can be considered as a single model with two sub-units, with the latent embedding space as an interface between them. It would have been better to train the whole model, hence both sub-units, together. This raises the question of joining mixed model and neural network concepts in a single model, which is the topic of my post-doctoral research fellowship at CNRS. Mixed-effect neural networks (MENN) have already been investigated (Xiong et al. 2019; Simchoni and Rosset 2023); however, both approaches use a non-restricted likelihood loss resulting in biased variance estimates. The variances are both a quantity of interest, and the amount of shrinkage that regulates the BLUPs, so obtaining unbiased estimates is therefore pivotal. Exploring whether REML can be carried over to such models first required a REML solver that lives in the same computational world as neural networks: differentiable, and running on GPU.

5.1 pyreml: solving mixed models by REML gradient descent
Throughout the research described in the previous sections, I lacked an open-source, frequentist REML implementation allowing complex specifications such as kinships, multivariate and random regression structures, heteroscedastic residuals, and factor-analytic rank reduction. pyreml was developed to fill this gap (Marchal, Trottier, et al. 2026), with an uncommon approach. Most REML solvers are based on the expectation-maximization (EM) or average-information (AI) algorithms, which are well suited to estimating mixed model variances. pyreml, instead, builds a differentiable PyTorch graph of the REML loss and minimizes it by gradient descent. This lets PyTorch run the model resolution on GPU, greatly accelerating the computation. With some optimization (see the doc), notably replacing some automatic differentiation by closed forms and automatically using the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury identity when advantageous, pyreml running on GPU outperforms the state-of-the-art software Wombat running on CPU, on a dense GBLUP benchmark of increasing size (Figure 11).






Figure 11: Benchmark comparing the computation time of pyreml to Wombat on a GBLUP of increasing \(n\) simulated individuals, with a single observation by individual. Both genetic and residual variances taken as \(10\) and initiated at \(1\). pyreml runs on 2 different GPUs (L40S and A100), both on float64 (“double”) numerical resolution and a custom (“mixed”) strategy consisting in pre-heating with float32 and finishing on float64. Wombat runs on \(64\) CPUs, and 3 algorithms are tested: AI (average information), EM (expectation-maximization) and PX-AI (a mix of parameter expansion and AI). EM was not run after \(n > 5000\) as it was very slow, and all variance estimates and BLUP accuracies were identical across software, hardware and methods except for AI with \(n \geq 10000\) (from Marchal, Trottier, et al. 2026).



Three aspects of this benchmark deserve attention beyond raw speed. First, the comparison is deliberately set on each tool’s own hardware: Wombat on a 64-CPU machine with its three algorithms, pyreml on GPU. Second, the “mixed” strategy is specific to the GPU world, as most commercial GPUs such as L40S are optimized for float32 computation. The strategy consists in warming up in single precision and finishing in double precision, without loss on the final estimates. It is useless, even slightly counterproductive, on float64 GPUs such as A100. Third, all methods converged to identical variance estimates and BLUP accuracies, except AI for \(n \geq 10000\). This echoes the fragility of AI-REML already met with oil palm and larch (Section 2): the algorithm is fast when it works, but it can derail, whereas gradient descent on the REML loss converged to the common solution in all cases.
The genomic simulations were carried out using the package meiosim (Marchal and Raimondi 2026), which we developed for this purpose. We pushed pyreml further and analyzed \(25000\) simulated A. thaliana genotypes across 40 environments in a complete block design (i.e. 1 million observations), with \(h^2 = 0.01\), the 40 environments being both simulated and analyzed as heteroscedastic. The analysis ran in 279 seconds on an A100 GPU.
The point of pyreml is not to out-engineer the reference frequentist software (ASReml, Wombat, BLUPF90, etc.) on their own ground, decades of algorithmic refinement on CPU, but to bring REML where these tools cannot go: GPU hardware and differentiable graphs. This is also the necessary condition for any attempt to couple REML with neural networks, which are trained by gradient descent on GPU.


5.2 Perspective
Neural networks are gaining popularity in genomic prediction and breeding (Raimondi et al. 2022; Cooper et al. 2025). This can be explained by their ability to take whole genome sequences as input, by their flexibility, and by the performance they demonstrate in all fields of data science around us. Mixed models, for their part, benefit from theoretical optimality properties, and above all from the consistency between their outputs and their uses in genetics: a breeding value, a heritability or a genetic correlation has a meaning, beyond the raw predictive ability. Moreover, the mixed model framework has been the fertile ground for many methodological developments in breeding, such as active learning (Rincent et al. 2012; Heslot and Feoktistov 2017), interpretability (Gualdrón Duarte et al. 2014), and short-term (Lehermeier et al. 2017) and long-term (De Beukelaer et al. 2017) genetic diversity management.
I do not see these two frameworks as competitors, and the question is how far they can be merged without losing what makes mixed model parameters meaningful.
Neural networks already commonly use regularization, for instance by adding to the training loss the squared norm of the weights, scaled by a constant. This is the penalty of ridge regression, and it amounts to assuming that the weights are normally distributed with a fixed variance. In a mixed model, this is precisely the role of the random effect variances, with one difference: they are not set by hand, but estimated from the data by REML, and they determine the amount of shrinkage of the BLUPs. Learning the amount of regularization in this way remains uncommon in neural networks, and is a concrete path for carrying mixed model concepts over to them.
Biological questions are open too: heritability, genetic correlations and reaction norms are defined within a linear, additive model, and their meaning in a learned, non-linear genotype–phenotype map remains to be established. How can the prediction of long-term genetic gain, stacking favorable alleles from generation to generation, benefit from the predictive power of deep neural networks? How can this apply to the complexity of evolutionary biology, where all phenotypic traits and their plasticity are simultaneously selected in a rapidly changing biotic and abiotic environment? How can an over-parameterized model draw generalizable and interpretable pathways through a virtually infinite number of epistatic combinations?
Whatever the outcome, exploring these questions would clarify what quantitative genetics can expect from deep learning. They also connect to explainable AI: where most explainability methods interpret a trained network a posteriori, the mixed model is understandable by construction, as it decomposes the phenotype into components whose role is explicit. This is the research program I intend to develop in the coming years: models as expressive as neural networks, and as understandable as mixed models.

title: Alexandre Marchal
text:
My research revolves around a single object: the genetic covariance matrix, which describes how phenotypes co-vary across traits and environments through inheritance, and how individuals resemble each other, whether through pedigree, markers or, more recently, learned representations. I develop statistical methods to estimate it when it becomes large and complex, and I use it to understand how phenotypes are built: phenotypic plasticity, trade-offs between traits, components of heterosis. This places my work at the interface of quantitative genetics, statistical modeling and machine learning.



Research



Publications



Curriculum




Main contributions

Differentiable REML on GPU. I developed pyreml, a mixed model library that fits REML by direct differentiation of its loss in PyTorch. Running on GPU, it outperforms the state-of-the-art mixed model solver Wombat on a dense GBLUP benchmark. Its differentiable design makes it a building block for further developments such as mixed effects neural networks.
Factor-analytic mixed models. With a Master’s student I supervised, I developed a Bayesian implementation of the FA model, then integrated a frequentist version in pyreml: as far as I know, the first open-source REML implementation of the FA mixed model. We illustrated, as a proof of concept, that the kinship can be replaced by a similarity built from neural network embeddings, opening variance decomposition to non-genetic applications (text, images, etc.).
Phenotypic plasticity and heterosis. Using Bayesian random regression along a water-availability gradient, I demonstrated that hybrid larch heterosis, individual genetic contrasts and a growth–density trade-off were all amplified under favorable environmental conditions.
Multivariate genetic models. During my MSc internship, I showed that modeling two correlated yield components jointly improved oil palm selection accuracy, even without the extreme heritability or missing-data patterns usually invoked to justify multivariate models. For hybrid larch, I fitted a 6-trait Bayesian model and characterized the marginal priors induced by parameter expansion, which had not been assessed before.



Trajectory
After a PhD in quantitative genetics at INRAE-Orléans (2014–2018), I spent ~5 years in the genomic breeding industry and 3 years as a data science consultant. I then returned to academia as a post-doc researcher at IGMM — CNRS, where I work on integrating mixed model concepts into neural network models for genomic prediction.
I have taught 700+ hours, starting with science tutoring during my studies (197 hours), then as a teaching assistant at the University of Orléans during my PhD (128 hours), and in professional training (about 378 hours). I have also supervised 4 MSc interns.
